title: How Senior Leaders Can Support Subject Leaders
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart addresses a structural problem in primary school leadership: subject leaders are asked to drive curriculum quality across an entire discipline while typically receiving minimal non-contact time, and senior leaders often fail to give them the specific support that would make the role sustainable. He organizes his argument around five concrete responsibilities senior leaders should own rather than delegate entirely to the subject leader: setting clear strategic direction on questions like whether subjects are taught discretely or through topics, protecting subject leaders' attention by acting as 'gatekeepers' when ten-plus subject leads compete for the same teacher time, and simply making time available to read, think, and observe. Hart's most concrete practical suggestion addresses a common gap-filling problem — a subject leader who lacks deep expertise in their subject — by recommending senior leaders bring in outside specialists, such as a local artist or musician, to help map end-point goals and sequencing rather than leaving an under-expert leader to guess. He closes by contrasting a common reactive model of subject leadership (monitor, observe, report at a staff meeting) with a proactive alternative in which leaders get ahead of units of work by gathering resources before teachers need them, arguing the reactive model risks producing feedback that is 'redundant' by the time teachers can act on it.
points: Hart's 'gatekeeper' framing — senior leaders must actively prioritize which of ten-plus competing subject leaders 'take the light' at a given time — names a coordination problem schools routinely leave unmanaged, letting subject leaders compete unproductively for the same teacher attention.

His concrete fix for expertise gaps (bringing in a local artist or musician to help map end-point goals when no staff member has deep subject knowledge) offers a practical, low-cost solution to a problem many schools treat as unsolvable without hiring a specialist teacher.

The contrast between reactive subject leadership ('monitor, then report at a staff meeting after the unit has already moved on') and proactive subject leadership (gathering resources ahead of upcoming units) reframes the timing of support, not just its content, as the key lever for making subject-leader feedback actually usable.
quotes: Subject leaders are the engine room of school improvement and the support that senior leaders provide can make all the difference to their success.

At any one time there might 10+ subject leaders all vying for teachers' attention because they care about their subject but teachers cannot work on developing their practice in all at once. Senior leaders need to be the gatekeepers, prioritising which subjects take the light and which take a back seat at different points in time.
It can be tempting to push subject leaders straight into some sort of monitoring or more formal evaluation but this is a mistake.
No-one with art expertise? Work with a local artist to map out the end point pieces and the sequences of learning required to get there.

5 ways for senior leaders to support subject leaders: Provide clear strategic direction. Direct their attention to what matters. Make time. Make the most of expertise. Help them to be proactive as well as responsive.
